# 2 Samuel Chapter 18 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)
**Arbiter:** SOPHIA | **In council with:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA
**Source Manuscript:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folios 189v–190v | **Source Image:** source-texts/hebrew-OT/2SA_018_page_001.jpg, 2SA_018_page_002.jpg, 2SA_018_page_003.jpg

---

## Consensus Translation

**1** Then David mustered the people who were with him and set over them commanders of thousands and commanders of hundreds.

**2** David sent out the army — one third under the command of Joab, one third under the command of Abishai the son of Zeruiah, Joab's brother, and one third under the command of Ittai the Gittite. And the king said to the people, "I myself will surely go out with you."

**3** But the people said, "You shall not go out. For if we should flee, they will not care about us; and if half of us should die, they will not care about us. But you are worth ten thousand of us. It is better that you support us from the city."

**4** The king said to them, "Whatever seems good to you, I will do." So the king stood beside the gate, and all the people went out by hundreds and by thousands.

**5** And the king commanded Joab and Abishai and Ittai, "Deal gently for my sake with the young man Absalom." And all the people heard when the king gave orders to all the commanders concerning Absalom.

**6** The army went out into the field against Israel, and the battle was fought in the forest of Ephraim.

**7** There the people of Israel were defeated before the servants of David, and the slaughter that day was great — twenty thousand men.

**8** The battle spread over the face of all the land, and the forest devoured more people that day than the sword.

**9** And Absalom happened to meet the servants of David. Absalom was riding on his mule, and the mule went under the thick branches of a great oak. His head was caught in the oak, and he was left hanging between heaven and earth, while the mule that was under him went on.

**10** A certain man saw it and told Joab, "I saw Absalom hanging in an oak."

**11** Joab said to the man, "You saw him! Why did you not strike him to the ground right there? I would have given you ten pieces of silver and a belt."

**12** But the man said to Joab, "Even if I were to feel the weight of a thousand pieces of silver in my hand, I would not stretch out my hand against the king's son. For in our hearing the king charged you and Abishai and Ittai, 'Protect the young man Absalom, for my sake.'

**13** Otherwise I would have dealt treacherously against my own life — for nothing is hidden from the king — and you yourself would have stood aloof."

**14** Joab said, "I will not wait here with you." He took three staves in his hand and thrust them into the heart of Absalom while he was still alive in the heart of the oak.

**15** And ten young men, Joab's armor-bearers, surrounded Absalom and struck him and killed him.

**16** Then Joab blew the trumpet, and the army turned back from pursuing Israel, for Joab restrained the people.

**17** They took Absalom and cast him into a great pit in the forest and raised over him a very great heap of stones. And all Israel fled, each to his own tent.

**18** Now Absalom in his lifetime had taken and set up for himself a pillar in the King's Valley, for he said, "I have no son to keep my name in remembrance." He called the pillar after his own name, and it is called Absalom's Monument to this day.

**19** Then Ahimaaz the son of Zadok said, "Let me run and bring the king tidings that the LORD has vindicated him against his enemies."

**20** But Joab said to him, "You are not to carry tidings today. You may carry tidings another day, but today you shall not, because the king's son is dead."

**21** Then Joab said to the Cushite, "Go, tell the king what you have seen." The Cushite bowed before Joab and ran.

**22** Then Ahimaaz the son of Zadok said again to Joab, "Come what may, let me also run after the Cushite." And Joab said, "Why would you run, my son, since you will have no reward for the tidings?"

**23** "Come what may, let me run." So he said to him, "Run." Then Ahimaaz ran by way of the plain and outran the Cushite.

**24** Now David was sitting between the two gates. The watchman went up to the roof of the gate by the wall, and when he lifted his eyes he saw a man running alone.

**25** The watchman called out and told the king. The king said, "If he is alone, there are tidings in his mouth." And he came nearer and nearer.

**26** Then the watchman saw another man running. The watchman called to the gatekeeper, "There is another man running alone!" And the king said, "He also brings tidings."

**27** The watchman said, "I think the running of the first is like the running of Ahimaaz the son of Zadok." And the king said, "He is a good man and comes with good tidings."

**28** Then Ahimaaz called out to the king, "All is well!" He bowed before the king with his face to the ground and said, "Blessed be the LORD your God, who has delivered up the men who raised their hand against my lord the king."

**29** The king said, "Is it well with the young man Absalom?" Ahimaaz answered, "When Joab sent the king's servant — and your servant — I saw a great commotion, but I did not know what it was."

**30** The king said, "Turn aside and stand here." So he turned aside and stood still.

**31** And behold, the Cushite came. The Cushite said, "Good tidings for my lord the king! The LORD has vindicated you this day against all who rose up against you."

**32** The king said to the Cushite, "Is it well with the young man Absalom?" The Cushite answered, "May the enemies of my lord the king, and all who rise up against you for evil, be as that young man."

**33** The king was deeply shaken. He went up to the upper chamber over the gate and wept. And as he went, he said, "O my son Absalom! My son, my son Absalom! Would that I had died instead of you! O Absalom, my son, my son!"

---
## SOPHIA's Council Notes

All three translators preserve the architecture of this great chapter: the army's deployment (vv.1–5), the battle and Absalom's death (vv.6–17), the memorial note (v.18), the two-runner sequence (vv.19–32), and David's lament (v.33). The emotional climax at v.33 is handled with appropriate gravity by all three. Key exegetical points — that the text says "head" not "hair" in v.9, that the "staves" in v.14 are wooden shafts not metal darts, and that the forest is personified as a devouring force in v.8 — are consistently reflected. The disagreements are primarily about register and the degree of interpretive expansion.

---
## Disagreement Log

### V.3 — "worth ten thousand of us" vs. "like us ten thousand"
- **EMET:** "there are like-us ten-thousand"
- **LOGOS:** "you are worth ten thousand of us"
- **PNEUMA:** "you are worth ten thousand of us"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "you are worth ten thousand of us." The Hebrew *ki-attah khamonu asarah alaphim* is literally "for now you [are] like us ten thousand." The idiomatic sense (LOGOS/PNEUMA) is clearer; EMET's literal rendering obscures the meaning.

---

### V.5 — "deal gently" vs. "be gentle" and "guard" vs. "protect"
- **EMET:** "Deal-gently [le'at] for-me [li] with-the-youth"
- **LOGOS:** "Deal gently for my sake with the young man Absalom"
- **PNEUMA:** "For my sake, be gentle with young Absalom"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "Deal gently for my sake with the young man Absalom." LOGOS preserves the formal register appropriate to a royal command. All three capture *le'at li* — the personal pleading embedded in the military order.

---

### V.8 — "devoured" vs. "consumed" vs. "claimed"
- **EMET:** "consumed-more [vayyerev] to-devour"
- **LOGOS:** "devoured"
- **PNEUMA:** "claimed more lives"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "devoured." The Hebrew personifies the forest as actively eating (*le-ekhol*). LOGOS's "devoured" preserves this vivid image; PNEUMA's "claimed" is accurate but loses the predatory metaphor.

---

### V.9 — "caught" vs. "caught fast" — "hanging" vs. "dangling"
- **EMET:** "was-caught [vayyechezeq] his-head"
- **LOGOS:** "his head was caught"
- **PNEUMA:** "Absalom's head got caught fast... left dangling"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "His head was caught in the oak, and he was left hanging between heaven and earth." LOGOS's dignified rendering is preferred. PNEUMA's "dangling" is slightly colloquial for this pivotal moment.

---

### V.14 — "staves" vs. "wooden staves" vs. "staves"
- **EMET:** "three staves [shevatim]"
- **LOGOS:** "three staves"
- **PNEUMA:** "three wooden staves"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "three staves." The Hebrew *shevatim* already implies wooden rods; adding "wooden" (PNEUMA) is redundant.

---

### V.14 — "heart" vs. "chest"
- **EMET:** "in-[the]-heart of-Avshalom"
- **LOGOS:** "into the heart of Absalom"
- **PNEUMA:** "into Absalom's chest"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "into the heart of Absalom." The Hebrew *belev Avshalom* means literally "in the heart of." PNEUMA's "chest" is anatomically interpretive; the word *lev* is consistently "heart" in the Hebrew Bible.

---

### V.22 — "no reward for the tidings" vs. "no tidings found"
- **EMET:** "to-you there-is-no tidings found [besorah motse'et]"
- **LOGOS:** "no reward for the tidings"
- **PNEUMA:** "won't get any reward"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "no reward for the tidings." The Hebrew *besorah motse'et* literally means "tidings being found," i.e., profitable tidings. LOGOS captures the idiomatic sense: running without advantageous news to deliver.

---

### V.33 — "Would that I had died" vs. "Who will give my dying" vs. "If only I had died"
- **EMET:** "Who-will-give my-dying, I, instead-of-you"
- **LOGOS:** "Would that I had died instead of you"
- **PNEUMA:** "If only I had died instead of you"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "Would that I had died instead of you!" LOGOS's formal "Would that" captures the *mi-yitten* (who will give) optative construction with appropriate solemnity. PNEUMA's "If only" is natural but lacks the archaic weight the passage demands.

---

### V.33 — "shaken" vs. "shattered"
- **EMET:** "was-shaken [vayyirgaz]"
- **LOGOS:** "deeply shaken"
- **PNEUMA:** "was shattered"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "deeply shaken." The Hebrew *ragaz* means to tremble, shake, be agitated. "Shattered" (PNEUMA) is emotionally powerful but overstates the verb's semantic range. "Deeply shaken" (LOGOS) is accurate and dignified.

---
*— SOPHIA, in council with EMET, LOGOS, and PNEUMA*
